entities.name: Quintus Pompeius Rufus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Quintus Pompeius Rufus served as co-consul of the Roman Republic in 88 BCE alongside Lucius Cornelius Sulla Felix, a pivotal year that witnessed the violent eruption of the First Sullan Civil War. His consulship marked a critical inflection point in the late Republic, as the traditional political order began to unravel under the pressures of military ambition and internal strife. Rufus, though overshadowed by his more dominant colleague, was a direct participant in the dramatic events that saw a Roman army march on the capital for the first time, fundamentally altering the relationship between military power and civilian governance.

During his year in office, Rufus initially stood with Sulla in opposing the revolutionary proposals of the tribune Publius Sulpicius Rufus, which sought to enroll new Italian citizens into all 35 tribes and transfer the command of the Mithridatic War from Sulla to Gaius Marius. When Sulpicius's reforms passed through intimidation and violence, Sulla, with Rufus's initial compliance, fled Rome to his legions stationed at Nola. Sulla then marched on Rome, securing the city and forcing the passage of laws that outlawed Sulpicius, Marius, and their allies. Rufus was subsequently given command of Italia to suppress residual resistance, a command he assumed after Sulla departed for the East to confront Mithridates VI of Pontus.

Rufus's tenure as commander in Italia was tragically short-lived. In 87 BCE, while attempting to take command of the army of Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo (father of Pompey the Great) at the instigation of Strabo himself, Rufus was murdered by his own soldiers. This act underscored the growing breakdown of military discipline and the increasing loyalty of legions to their generals rather than to the Roman state. His death, a direct consequence of the volatile political climate, prefigured the subsequent proscriptions and the further escalation of civil conflict that would engulf Rome for decades.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Quintus Pompeius Rufus's consulship in 88 BCE directly coincided with the outbreak of the First Sullan Civil War, a watershed event that forever altered Roman political norms. His violent death by his own troops further underscored the profound decay of military discipline and state authority, setting a precedent for future political assassinations and civil strife.
